hero_deck: Lima's airport had never charged international transfer passengers a fee. I designed the web channel to collect it, one of four ways to pay, and handed it over.
hero_role1: Roles — Internal consultant · UX/UI designer · Planning coordinator
hero_role3: Scope — Planning → UX/UI design → prototyping → evaluation → handoff
hero_rv_txt: A passenger lands in Lima and connects to another international flight. At the new terminal they owe a fee the airport had never charged, and no channel existed to collect it. Five central areas each held a piece of the problem. As the internal consultant from Processes and Innovation, I coordinated the planning between them, designed the web payment flow, evaluated it and handed it to the team that built it. TUUA Transfer runs today, charging 130,000+ international transfer passengers a month.
act0_verdict: A new fee, with no precedent to copy.
act0_lede: Switch channels to follow an international transfer passenger through the fee.
act0_rv1: Jorge Chávez. Lima's international airport, run by the private operator Lima Airport Partners, where I worked.
act0_rv2: International transfer passenger. A passenger who arrives in Lima on an international flight and connects to another international flight.
act0_rv3: TUUA. Tarifa Unificada de Uso de Aeropuerto, the airport-use fee. TUUA Transfer is the one charged for the services these passengers use while they board.
act0_j3: Pass the eGate and the TUUA turnstile
act0_tp_web: A QR code by email. The passenger pays on the web platform and shows the QR code at the eGate.
act0_tp_staff: A bar-code sticker. At any of the three staffed points, the passenger receives a sticker on the boarding pass, which the eGate reads.
act0_s1_p: Charged today, on a platform a third party operates.
act0_s2_p: Nobody had charged this fee before, inside the airport or outside it.
act1_verdict: A fee with no way to collect it.
act1_lede: Three links, and the middle one missing.
act1_foot: Five central areas each held a piece of it: Finance, Airport Operations, IT, Commercial and Reputation.
act2_verdict: Five central areas at the table. I coordinated, I did not own.
act2_lede: Where I sat between the areas that shaped the fee.
act2_c1_x: Finance, Airport Operations, IT, Commercial and Reputation each held a piece of the fee.
act2_c2_x: I was the internal consultant from Processes and Innovation. I coordinated the planning across the five central areas, delivered the design work and advised in the decision meetings.
act2_c3_t: What the charter says about me
act2_c3_x: The client sat in another internal area, and the programme charter's stakeholder table does not list me as owner. That is the accurate record and this page keeps it.
act2_synth: The planning I coordinated held across all five central areas through launch.

act4_rv_txt: The web platform is one of four ways to pay the fee, and the only digital one. On the web, the passenger receives a QR code by email and shows it at the eGate. At the three staffed channels, the passenger receives a bar-code sticker on the boarding pass instead.
act5_verdict: My part ended where the build began.
act5_lede: How the proposal was evaluated, and where it stopped.
act5_c1_x: Stakeholder review sessions for the digital platform, and field observation at the physical payment booths, evidenced by two pre-trial surveys and a set of qualitative notes. They are different methods answering different questions, and neither stands in for the other.
act5_c2_x: The same closure mail states that development would add one to two screens beyond the ones I proposed, with minor adjustments, gated on Billing's approval of the final version. The line between my deliverable and the vendor's is written into the programme's own documents, not only into my account of it.
act5_c3_x: Setting the fee was never my decision, and neither were the platform's build, deployment or operation. A third party operates it today.
act6_verdict: The platform is live, it is not mine, and the difference between what I proposed and what shipped is public.
act6_lede: A year later, I reviewed the live platform against my own proposal.
act6_method: Public, unauthenticated pages only. No transaction was submitted, no session was captured, and no data was collected beyond what any visitor sees.
act6_f1_txt: Personal data first: name and email, a validation code, then payment and the ticket.
act6_f2_txt: The flight first: an eligibility self-declaration, flight details with the fee, then customer details before the payment control.
act6_bridge: Reordered, not removed. Personal-data capture now follows the flight lookup, and I measured it doing exactly that on the customer-details screen. I read the reordering as intuitive and do not contest it.
act6_scan1: Four screens are reachable before the payment control itself: the homepage, an eligibility self-declaration, a flight-details screen carrying the fee, and a customer-details screen. The pass stops there, deliberately, one control short of paying.
act6_scan2: The fee is set at $11.86, shown a full screen earlier than I proposed and consistent between its two appearances: $23.72 for two passengers. Fee-setting was never my decision.
act6_scan3: Eligibility is gated by a self-declaration click — "Soy ese tipo de pasajero" — rather than the automatic agreement check the technical scope specified. To my own knowledge of the build, that check was never implemented as written. This pass could not see past its own boundary to confirm it.
act6_findings: Six findings: one major, five minor, none critical. The major one is a screen headed "Ingresa tus datos personales y de tu vuelo" whose only fields are flight data.
act6_synth: I can read the gap between proposal and build in public, which is a better position than having to describe it.
act6_sequel: What I can claim: the design, prototype, evaluation and handoff of a platform live today. What I can't: its build, deployment or operation. What's next: six findings, one of them major, recorded for whoever runs it.
act3_notice: TUUA Transfer. I understand the platform's mechanism and contributed to its UX/UI design — not its development, deployment or operation.
